title: Revenue Leakage in Behavioral Health: Where SUD and Mental Health Programs Lose Money, and How to Measure It
summary: Where behavioral health and SUD programs lose revenue, with a metric, formula and worked example for each leak, HFMA definitions and a monthly scorecard.
body_markdown:
Revenue leakage in behavioral health is revenue a program earned but never collects: services delivered and never billed, residential or IOP days that run past an authorization, denials nobody works, payments below the contracted rate, claims written off for timely filing, and balances lost when a patient's Medicaid coverage ends. You find it by measuring each stage of the revenue cycle with a short list of formulas, most of them already defined in HFMA's MAP Keys, counted in dollars and reviewed on one scorecard every month.


Most practices say denials are the biggest hole. In a January 2026 MGMA Stat poll, 48% of medical group leaders named denials and appeals their largest source of revenue leakage, ahead of front-end issues (23%), billing and collections (14%), coding (13%) and charge posting (2%). SUD and mental health programs add leaks of their own: per diem days outside an approval, group sessions attended but never charged, and patients who lose Medicaid mid-treatment. Below is a leakage map with ten stages; for each, the metric, the formula, a worked example (every number in the examples is hypothetical), where the data lives and the fix, then a one-page monthly scorecard.


The short version


- Leakage is the gap between what your contracts and documentation support and what you collect. The contractual adjustment your contract requires is not leakage; a denial you never appealed is.
- Measure ten stages: eligibility, authorizations, documentation, charge capture, coding, denial follow-up, underpayments, timely filing, patient balances and Medicaid coverage churn.
- Use standard definitions where they exist. HFMA's MAP Keys define clean claim rate, remittance denial rate, denial write-offs, bad debt and days in A/R.
- Count dollars, not lines, and tag every loss to a root cause and an owner.
- Published benchmarks are not behavioral health specific. MGMA puts first-submission denials for medical groups at 7% to 8% over the past four years; treat outside numbers as context and track your own trend.


## What counts as revenue leakage


Start from expected net revenue: what each service should pay under the contract or fee schedule, given what was documented. Leakage is everything between that number and cash collected that you could have prevented or recovered. It includes unbilled services, preventable denials written off, underpayments, timely filing write-offs, avoidable bad debt and services delivered after coverage ended. It excludes the contractual allowance. X12 reason code 45 ("charge exceeds fee schedule/maximum allowable or contracted/legislated fee arrangement") is normally the contract working as written, but only if the allowed amount actually matches the contract, which is why underpayment review matters.


Separate leakage from delay. Rising days in A/R costs cash flow; leakage costs revenue. Track both, but do not let a good days-in-A/R number hide money that will never arrive. The two disciplines that own these problems overlap; our piece on[revenue integrity vs. revenue cycle management](https://blog.adentris.com/revenue-integrity-vs-revenue-cycle-management/) explains who usually owns what.


## The behavioral health leakage map


Stage How BH and SUD programs leak Where the data lives


**1. Eligibility and benefits** Inactive coverage, BH benefit carved out to another plan, coverage changed between visits 270/271 responses, intake records, 835 remits


**2. Authorizations** Days or units past the approval, missed concurrent reviews, step-downs billed under the old approval Utilization review log, EHR census, 835


**3. Documentation** Level of care not justified, stale treatment plan, missing signatures Chart audits, 835 reason and remark codes


**4. Charge capture** Groups and family sessions attended but never charged, units that do not match minutes EHR attendance and schedule, charge register


**5. Coding** Wrong time code, diagnosis mismatch, modifier errors, edit failures Claim scrubber, 835


**6. Denial follow-up** Denials that age out unworked 835, denial work queue


**7. Underpayments** Paid below contract, old per diem rates still loaded 835 paid amounts, contract terms


**8. Timely filing** Claims held, rejected or corrected too late Practice management system, claim scrubber


**9. Patient balances** Copays and deductibles not collected, balances sent to bad debt Patient accounting, general ledger


**10. Medicaid churn** Coverage lost at renewal mid-treatment 271 responses, state portal, plan rosters


## Metrics, formulas and fixes by stage


### 1. Eligibility and benefits


**Metrics.** Insurance verification rate (HFMA MAP Key PA-3) = verified encounters / registered encounters. Eligibility denial dollars = denied dollars carrying reason codes such as 27 (expenses incurred after coverage terminated), 31 (patient cannot be identified as our insured), 109 (not covered by this payer) or 22 (may be covered by another payer).


**Example.** 1,840 of 2,000 registered encounters verified = 92%. Eligibility denials for the month: $18,400.


**Fix.** Verify before each admission or level-of-care change and on a schedule for recurring patients, and check behavioral health benefits specifically, not just active coverage. Our[BH denial codes guide](https://blog.adentris.com/behavioral-health-denial-codes-carc-guide/) lists the eligibility service type codes for mental health and substance use benefits.


### 2. Authorizations and concurrent reviews


**Metrics.** Service authorization rate (HFMA PA-5, outpatient) = encounters authorized before claim release / encounters requiring authorization, where HFMA builds the denominator as authorized encounters plus encounters denied for lack of authorization. For residential, PHP and IOP, add days at risk = days delivered minus days covered by a valid authorization.


**Example.** 1,800 residential patient days delivered; 1,710 fall inside valid approvals. 90 days at risk at a $700 per diem = $63,000 of revenue that depends on a retro-authorization or an appeal.


**Fix.** Calendar every concurrent review, request extensions before the window closes, and log request time, decision time, reference number and reviewer. Our free[prior authorization request log](https://adentris.com/resources/templates/prior-auth-request-log?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=behavioral-health-revenue-leakage-metrics&utm_content=inline) tracks requests, decisions and next review dates in one sheet. Denials here arrive as reason code 197 (authorization absent) or 198 (authorization exceeded).


### 3. Documentation and medical necessity


**Metrics.** Medical necessity denial rate = dollars denied with reason code 50 / dollars billed. Pre-bill documentation pass rate = charts that pass every applicable check / charts reviewed.


**Example.** 340 of 400 charts pass = 85%. $22,000 denied with code 50 on $900,000 billed = 2.4%.


**Fix.** Check charts before billing and repair the template fields that fail most often. This leak also shows up later as audit recoupments, which never appear in denial reports. See our guides to[CO-50 appeals](https://blog.adentris.com/co-50-denial-medical-necessity-behavioral-health/) and[full-sweep chart audits in SUD](https://blog.adentris.com/chart-audit-sud-full-sweep-vs-sampling/) .


### 4. Charge capture and units


**Metrics.** Charge capture rate = services billed / billable services documented. Late charges as a percentage of total charges (HFMA CL-2) = gross charges posted more than 3 days after the service date / total gross charges. Total charge lag days (HFMA PB-4) = sum of days from service date to posting date / number of charge codes billed.


**Example.** Attendance logs show 2,600 billable group sessions; 2,470 were billed = 95%. 130 missing sessions at $40 each = $5,200.


**Fix.** Reconcile attendance to charges daily for every program, and derive units from documented minutes. For time-based therapy codes, see our[psychotherapy CPT time rules](https://blog.adentris.com/psychotherapy-cpt-codes-90832-90834-90837/) .


### 5. Coding and claim data


**Metrics.** Clean claim rate (HFMA CL-1) = claims that pass edits with no manual intervention / claims accepted into the claims processing tool. Coding denial rate = claims denied for coding reasons (for example reason codes 4, 11 and 236, and 151 when units exceed an edit) / claims remitted.


**Example.** 2,610 of 3,000 claims pass clean = 87%. 96 coding denials on 3,000 remitted claims = 3.2%.


**Fix.** Turn each recurring scrubber hold into a rule at the source. MGMA's January poll respondents also described widespread[undercoding](https://adentris.com/solutions/autonomous-coding?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=behavioral-health-revenue-leakage-metrics&utm_content=inline) , so audit for missed revenue as well as overcoding.


### 6. Denials not worked


**Metrics.** HFMA's Claim Integrity Task Force defines initial denial rate = initial denial claims / claims submitted (using the average of the three months before the reporting month), by volume and by dollars, counting only the first denial on each claim. Add denial follow-up rate = initial denials corrected or appealed / initial denials, the task force's percentage of initial denials overturned, and denial write-offs as a percentage of net patient service revenue (MAP Key AR-6) = net dollars written off as denials / average monthly net patient service revenue.


**Example.** 380 initial denials on 3,000 claims = 12.7%. 230 worked = 60.5%. $41,000 in denial write-offs on $820,000 average monthly net revenue = 5.0%.


**Fix.** Sort the work queue by dollars and filing deadline, tag each denial to a root cause, and send prevention back to the step that caused it.


### 7. Underpayments against contract


**Metrics.** Underpayment variance = sum of (contracted payment minus actual payment) on lines paid below contract. Underpayment rate = lines paid below contract / lines paid.


**Example.** An IOP per diem contracted at $250 is paid at $225 on 300 days after a fee schedule update was missed: $7,500 for the month, invisible inside the contractual adjustment.


**Fix.** Load your top payers' rates into an expected-payment table, compare every 835 line, and dispute variances inside the contract's window.


### 8. Timely filing


**Rules.** Medicare claims must be filed no later than one calendar year after the date of service (42 CFR 424.44). State Medicaid agencies must require claims within 12 months of the date of service (42 CFR 447.45). Managed care and commercial limits come from the plan and your contract.


**Metrics.** Timely filing write-offs = dollars written off with reason code 29. Days in discharged not submitted to payer (HFMA PB-3) = gross dollars not final billed plus final billed but not submitted / average daily gross patient service revenue.


**Example.** $96,000 sitting in holds and unbilled accounts / $40,000 average daily gross revenue = 2.4 days. Code 29 write-offs: $6,300.


**Fix.** Age unbilled and rejected claims against each payer's limit, not against the date of service alone.


### 9. Patient balances and bad debt


**Metrics.** Point-of-service cash collections (HFMA PA-7) = patient payments collected before, at or shortly after service (HFMA allows up to seven days after discharge) / total self-pay cash collected. Bad debt (HFMA AR-7) = bad debt provision on the income statement / gross patient service revenue.


**Example.** $38,000 collected at point of service / $95,000 total self-pay cash = 40%.


**Fix.** Give estimates before admission and collect at intake. MGMA respondents tied this leak to high deductibles and rising patient responsibility.


### 10. Medicaid coverage churn


**Rules.** Medicaid eligibility based on MAGI income rules is renewed every 12 months today, and a person terminated for not returning renewal paperwork can be reconsidered without a new application if they submit it within 90 days, or longer if the state allows (42 CFR 435.916). Section 71107 of Public Law 119-21 moves most Medicaid expansion adults to renewals every 6 months, beginning with renewals scheduled on or after January 1, 2027, and CMS notes that the same law limits retroactive eligibility for that group to a maximum of one month before the month of application, for applications made on or after January 1, 2027. Our[Medicaid work requirements guide](https://blog.adentris.com/medicaid-work-requirements-behavioral-health/) covers what else changes.


**Metrics.** Coverage loss rate = active Medicaid patients whose coverage ended in the month / active Medicaid patients at the start of the month. Post-termination exposure = dollars billed for services after a coverage end date.


**Example.** 14 of 280 Medicaid patients lost coverage = 5%; $11,200 of services fell after the end dates.


**Fix.** Track renewal dates, help patients complete renewals, and re-verify Medicaid patients monthly.


## Two summary metrics that tell you whether fixes reach cash


Net days in A/R (HFMA FM-1) = net patient A/R on the balance sheet / average daily net patient service revenue over the last three months. MGMA describes days in A/R more simply as total A/R divided by average daily charges; either works if you never switch. Cash collection as a percentage of net patient service revenue (HFMA FM-2) = patient service cash collected / average monthly net patient service revenue. In a July 2026 MGMA Stat poll, 43% of medical group leaders said days in A/R were about the same as a year earlier, 32% said higher and 22% lower.


## Benchmarks: what is published, and how to use it


- **MGMA** says its benchmarking puts first-submission denials for medical groups at 7% to 8% across the past four years, and that its 2025 data suggests practices can push the rate below 5% with targeted process fixes.
- **Premier** , surveying hospitals and health systems on 2022 claims, found nearly 15% of claims submitted to private payers were initially denied, 54.3% of those denials were ultimately overturned and paid, and fighting a denial cost an average of $43.84 per claim.
- **HFMA** publishes the MAP Key definitions openly; benchmark values come through its subscriber tool.


None of these is specific to behavioral health or SUD, and none uses your payer mix. Use them to sanity-check, set your own three-month baseline, and judge yourself on direction.


## The one-page monthly leakage scorecard


Metric Formula Owner


Insurance verification rate Verified encounters / registered encounters Intake


Eligibility denial dollars Denied dollars with codes 27, 31, 109, 22 Intake


Authorization rate Authorized before claim release / requiring authorization Utilization review


Days at risk Days delivered minus days under valid approval Utilization review


Documentation pass rate Charts passing all checks / charts reviewed Clinical director, compliance


Medical necessity denial rate Code 50 dollars / billed dollars Compliance


Charge capture rate Services billed / billable services documented Billing


Clean claim rate Claims passing edits untouched / claims accepted Billing


Initial denial rate Initial denials / claims submitted (volume and dollars) Revenue cycle director


Denial follow-up rate Denials corrected or appealed / initial denials Billing


Denial write-offs Net denial write-offs / average monthly net revenue CFO


Underpayment variance Sum of contract minus paid on short-paid lines Billing, contracting


Timely filing write-offs Code 29 dollars Billing


Point-of-service collections POS payments / total self-pay cash Front desk


Bad debt Bad debt / gross patient service revenue CFO


Medicaid coverage loss rate Coverage ended / active Medicaid patients Intake


Net days in A/R Net A/R / average daily net revenue CFO


Put this month, last month and the three-month average beside each line, split the dollar lines by payer and level of care, and flag any line that worsens two months in a row.

## How to run the first measurement


1. **Pull 90 days of 835 remits** with group code, reason and remark codes, payer and service code on every adjustment line.
2. **Separate patient responsibility** (group code PR) from provider-liable lines and rank the rest by dollars.
3. **Reconcile one program** : attendance against charges, and census against approvals.
4. **Load three payer contracts** into an expected-payment table and compare paid amounts.
5. **Tag every loss** to one of the ten stages and an owner.
6. **Fix the top two sources** , then re-measure next month on the scorecard.

## Frequently asked questions


**What is revenue leakage in healthcare?**


Revenue leakage is revenue an organization earned but does not collect, such as services never billed, denials written off without appeal, payments below the contracted rate, timely filing write-offs and avoidable bad debt. Contractual allowances required by a payer contract are not leakage.


**How do you calculate clean claim rate?**


HFMA's MAP Key CL-1 divides the number of claims that pass edits with no manual intervention by the number of claims accepted into the claims processing tool for billing, for the month the claims are scrubbed. Print-and-mail claims are excluded.


**What is a good claim denial rate?**


There is no published behavioral health standard. MGMA reports first-submission denials for medical groups at 7% to 8% over the past four years and says its data suggests practices can get below 5%. A Premier survey of hospitals found nearly 15% of claims to private payers initially denied. Set a baseline from your own last three months and track the trend.


**How do you calculate days in A/R?**


HFMA's MAP Key FM-1 divides net patient A/R by average daily net patient service revenue over the most recent three months. MGMA describes days in A/R as total A/R divided by average daily charges. Pick one method and keep it.


**What is the difference between a denial and an underpayment?**


A denial pays nothing on a claim or line and carries a reason code that says why. An underpayment pays the claim, but for less than the contract requires, and often sits inside the contractual adjustment, so it only shows up when you compare paid amounts with contracted rates.


**How will Medicaid changes in 2027 affect behavioral health revenue?**


Under Public Law 119-21, most Medicaid expansion adults move to eligibility renewals every 6 months for renewals scheduled on or after January 1, 2027, and retroactive eligibility for that group is limited to one month before the month of application for applications made on or after that date. More renewals and less retro coverage mean more chances for services to fall after a coverage end date, so track renewal dates and re-verify monthly.
